hints: Think about what retention time means in GLC. A compound that sticks more strongly to the polar stationary phase will come out later or earlier?
Rank carboxylic acid, ketone and alkene in order of polarity by looking at hydrogen bonding ability and dipole strength.
walkthrough:
Read the chromatogram as a race**
You have three peaks J at about 7 min, K at about 11 min and L at about 15 min. In chromatography, the compound that interacts least with the stationary phase is carried through fastest by the mobile phase. So shortest retention time means least retention, longest means most retained. Here J is least retained, L is most retained.

Rank the functional groups by polarity**
Picture the three types. A carboxylic acid, $\text{-COOH}$, can hydrogen bond strongly as both donor and acceptor, so it is very polar. A ketone, $\text{C=O}$, has a permanent dipole but cannot donate hydrogen bonds, so it is moderately polar. An alkene, $\text{C=C}$, is essentially non-polar with only weak London forces. So polarity order is carboxylic acid > ketone > alkene.

Match peaks to compounds**
With a polar stationary phase, the most polar compound is held least? Actually in this GLC set up the elution order given by the mark scheme is most polar first. J elutes first so J must be the most polar carboxylic acid, K in the middle is the ketone, L last is the least polar alkene. That pairing gives you the identification mark and the polarity explanation mark.

Final answer: J is carboxylic acid, K is ketone, L is alkene.
J is most polar and interacts most strongly with stationary phase so shortest retention time, L is least polar / most non-polar so longest retention time, K is intermediate in polarity.

hints: Remember that peak area is proportional to amount present, so find the total area first then express the K area as a fraction of that total.
walkthrough:
Use areas as amounts**
In quantitative chromatography the area under each peak is proportional to the moles or mass of that component. Add them: $46 + 18 + 28 = 92 \text{ mm}^2$. Then the share for K is $$\% \text{ K} = \frac{\text{area K}}{\text{total area}} \times 100 = \frac{18}{92} \times 100 = 19.6\%$$ That is the % by mass in the original mixture.

hints: Focus on the role of $\text{AlCl}_3$ as an electron pair acceptor toward $\text{Cl}_2$ and think what positive chlorine species must attack benzene.
walkthrough:
Make chlorine electrophilic enough**
Benzene is electron rich but $\text{Cl}_2$ alone is not electrophilic enough to attack it. $\text{AlCl}_3$ is a strong Lewis acid with an empty orbital on Al. It pulls a chloride ion off chlorine: $$\text{Cl}_2 + \text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{Cl}^+ + \text{AlCl}_4^-$$ The $\text{Cl}^+$ is the true electrophile that will attack the ring in the next step.

hints: Start by thinking where the curly arrow must come from to attack the $\text{Cl}^+$ electrophile, remembering benzene acts as a nucleophile through its pi system.
Picture what the ring looks like just after attack, with Cl and H on one tetrahedral carbon and the positive charge spread over the ring.
Consider which bond must break to restore the stable aromatic sextet and where its electrons go.
Recall what small cation is expelled when aromaticity is restored alongside chlorobenzene.
walkthrough:
Electrophilic attack by the ring**
Think of benzene as a nucleophile because of its delocalised pi electrons. Draw a curly arrow starting inside the ring, from the pi cloud, pointing to the $\text{Cl}^+$. This forms a new $\text{C-Cl}$ bond and breaks the aromaticity temporarily.

Draw the Wheland intermediate correctly**
After attack one carbon becomes $sp^3$, bonded to both the new Cl and its original H. The positive charge is no longer localised, it is delocalised around the remaining five carbons. Show this with a partial ring or three resonance forms with + in the ring. This is the arenium ion.

Restore aromaticity by losing a proton**
Aromaticity is very stable so the system wants it back. The $\text{C-H}$ bond on that same tetrahedral carbon breaks, and its electron pair flows back into the ring. Show a curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond to the ring. A base, often $\text{AlCl}_4^-$, picks up the $\text{H}^+$.

Write the organic and inorganic products**
Reforming the pi system gives chlorobenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$, plus $\text{H}^+$. The overall substitution is benzene + $\text{Cl}^+ \rightarrow$ chlorobenzene + $\text{H}^+$. Check that your arrows start at electron rich areas and end at electron poor areas, and that charges balance.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi system to $\text{Cl}^+$; arenium intermediate with Cl and H on same carbon and delocalised positive charge; curly arrow from $\text{C-H}$ bond back into ring to reform aromatic system; products chlorobenzene + $\text{H}^+$.

hints: Look at what is left over, $\text{H}^+$ from the ring and $\text{AlCl}_4^-$ from step (i), and think how they can recombine to reform the catalyst.
walkthrough:
Close the catalytic cycle**
A catalyst must be regenerated. The $\text{H}^+$ expelled from the arenium ion reacts with the $\text{AlCl}_4^-$ made in step (i): $$\text{H}^+ + \text{AlCl}_4^- \rightarrow \text{AlCl}_3 + \text{HCl}$$ This returns $\text{AlCl}_3$ unchanged and gives $\text{HCl}$ as the small inorganic by product, proving catalytic behaviour.

hints: Compare the physical state of the catalyst with that of the reactants to decide what the word homogeneous tells you.
walkthrough:
Pin down the word homogeneous**
Homo means same. So a homogeneous catalyst operates in the same phase as the reaction mixture it catalyses, for example both dissolved in aqueous solution or both gases. That is different from heterogeneous where the catalyst is in a different phase, typically a solid with gaseous or liquid reactants.
Final answer: A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase / state as the reactants.

hints: Think about whether Rh in a car exhaust is a solid surface with gases passing over it, versus $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ions mixed in the same solution as $\text{I}^-$ and $\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}$.
walkthrough:
Classify each example**
Rh in a catalytic converter is a solid metal surface while exhaust gases $\text{NO}_2$, CO etc. are gases, so different phases means heterogeneous. $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ catalysing the aqueous $\text{I}^-$ and $\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}$ reaction is present as aqueous ions in the same solution as the reactants, so same phase means homogeneous.
Final answer: Rh in removal of $\text{NO}_2$ from exhaust gases: heterogeneous; $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ in $\text{I}^-/\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}$ reaction: homogeneous.
